newsitem.title: GERMANY: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND TAMES GARMISCH HILL FOR SECOND WIN.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-ALPHAND TAMES GARMISCH HILL FOR SECOND WIN.

text.p: France's Luc Alphand made skiing one of the most dangerous mountains on the World Cup circuit look easy as he sped to his fourth downhill victory of the season on Saturday.
After winning Friday's super-giant slalom in this German resort, the Frenchman roared down a bumpy, icy piste in one minute 54.27 seconds to win by more than half a second.

Italy's Pietro Vitalini, who had to ski twice after he was forced to stop his first run because a man got in his way on the piste, took second in 1:54.85 with compatriot Kristian Ghedina third one hundredth of a second further behind.

The Garmisch-Partenkirchen double marked a remarkable return to form for the 31-year-old Alphand after he crashed out of the downhill at this month's world championships in Sestriere and failed to figure in the super-G.
The performance even surprised the Frenchman who stretched his lead in both the overall World Cup standings and in the downhill standings where he is bidding for a third consecutive title.

"I don't know how I did it today. The piste was much harder than yesterday," Alphand said. "There was so much vibration on the course that it was difficult to control the skis. I didn't think I was so fast. I couldn't believe it at the finish."
The Garmisch hill has witnessed many crashes in the past. Three years ago former world champion Ulrike Maier was killed in a women's race on the Kandahar piste.
The course was even more difficult to ski in the mid-morning race on Saturday because parts of the piste were in the shade while others enjoyed bright sunshine.

Vitalini did well to avoid a crash in his first run when a man, not wearing skis, slid across the course and forced him to pull up. But the Italian kept his nerve, returned to the top of the mountain by helicopter and later raced down with confidence.

Ghedina, Alphand's main rival in the downhill World Cup, was happy to have taken third place and not lose too much ground on Alphand. The Frenchman now has an 111-point lead with two downhills remaining.
"I'm satisfied. It was a tough run with the shade and sun," the Italian said. "But it is going to be hard to beat Alphand this season," he said.
Alphand is bidding to become the first Frenchman to win the overall World Cup since Jean-Claude Killy in 1968. He has another chance to boost his lead in a further super-G in Garmisch on Sunday.
